name: Karl Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for your time, Karl. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Whatever you say stays confidential. Could you tell me about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Karl, I'm 58, and I lead the live-line crew for the electricity company along the coast, around the port. Live-line means we work on the wires while they're still switched on, with insulated sticks and gloves, so the hospital and the port don't lose power. My wife Ana is a receptionist at a dental practice, our son Tom's 31 and an accountant, and our daughter Bea is getting married in the spring, which is costing more than my first house did.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: We start with a tailboard talk at the depot by the old fish market, which is just the crew standing round the truck going over every step and every danger before we start. Then it's swapping insulators, fixing connections, sometimes moving a whole line over without switching it off. The salt air eats everything here, so there's always work. I like that it takes total focus, your mind can't wander. What wears me out is the dread before a big job, even after thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful gadget, like the satnav was, and leave it at that. At the depot we'd joke about it for a week and move on. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not much for online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as planned, which suits me. I'd work till about 63, pay for the wedding, and help the kids where I can. Ana and I would have a few good years before we're too old to enjoy them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. Keep working, keep saving, we've got about three months of bills put by, less after the wedding. I'd probably use the AI bits when they help and ignore them when they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Fine, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use any AI tools at the moment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. The company has a chatbot where you can look up a procedure, and it's quicker than flipping through the binder. And I used one to sort out a spreadsheet for Bea's wedding, which Ana thought was hilarious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you spend your last few working years on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring through my number two, Femi, he's ready to lead. I'd want the crew to keep its record, nobody hurt on live work in eleven years. That's the thing I'm proudest of.

S0.say: He'd say AI is a useful gadget, like satnav was, and leave it there. The depot would joke about it for a week and move on, and he wouldn't post anything.
S0.think: It means things stay as planned, which suits him: working to about 63, paying for his daughter's wedding and helping the kids. He and Ana would have a few good years afterwards.
S0.do: Keeps working and saving as usual, with about three months of bills put by, less after the wedding. Uses AI tools when they help and ignores them when they don't.
S0.quote: I used one to sort out a spreadsheet for Bea's wedding, which Ana thought was hilarious.
S0.fieldNote: Karl is a measured, practical man who uses AI occasionally, like a quicker procedure binder. The wedding is the big expense on his mind. He's proudest of eleven years without injury on live work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming whether we like it or not, so let's be sensible about it. Train people, don't panic, and check it's actually safe before you use it on live lines. That's what I'd say at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, I'd probably be fine. Live work is about as hands-on as it gets, and it would be a long time before anyone trusted a machine near an energised line. But I'd expect the company to use it as a reason to squeeze crews a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until the other depots had tried the new tools, then pick them up once they were working. I'd go on any training the company offered. And I'd watch the money a bit more closely, maybe trim the wedding budget a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but mostly steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you think would feel it first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office side. Planners, the people who do the switching schedules, the ones who sort the job paperwork. A lot of that is the kind of thing these programs are good at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you go further with the AI tools than you do now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once it's proven, yes. I don't want to be the first person testing something on a live line, but I don't want to be the last one who refuses either. Somewhere in the middle, that's me.

S1.say: He'd say it's coming whether people like it or not, so be sensible: train people, don't panic, and check it's safe before using it on live lines. That's what he'd say at work.
S1.think: He thinks he'd probably be fine, since live work is as hands-on as it gets and nobody will trust a machine near an energised line for a long time. But he expects the company to use it to squeeze crews.
S1.do: Waits until other depots have tried the new tools, then picks them up once they work, and goes on any training offered. Watches money more closely and trims the wedding budget a little.
S1.feel: A bit uneasy, but mostly steady.
S1.quote: I don't want to be the first person testing something on a live line, but I don't want to be the last one who refuses either.
S1.fieldNote: His steady, middle-of-the-road approach is clear: adopt once proven, not before. He expects office roles to feel it first. The wedding budget is already being nudged in his money thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for anyone to handle properly, and the government needs to slow it down where safety's at stake. I wouldn't blame any one group, it's just too fast. I'd say it calmly, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it worries me. I'd be 60, three years short of where I wanted to stop, and live-line work is exactly the dangerous stuff companies would most like a robot to do. That's the part that keeps me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting away a lot more straight away, maybe a third more each month. I'd talk to Bea about a smaller wedding, which would hurt. If the company offered a decent early package in the first year, I'd probably take it, and I'd look at whether my live-line training could get me work checking or certifying robot crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not falling apart, but properly anxious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd scale it back. Fewer guests, a cheaper venue, maybe the reception at Ana's sister's place. Bea would understand, she's sensible, but I'd feel I'd let her down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Femi?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to get on every course going and to make himself the guy who knows the machines. He's 39, he's got time. And I'd tell him that safety rules are written in blood, and not to let anyone forget that just because a robot's doing the job.

S2.say: He'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle properly and the government needs to slow it where safety is at stake. He wouldn't blame any one group, and he'd say it calmly.
S2.think: It worries him: he'd be 60, three years short of his planned stop, and live-line work is exactly the dangerous work companies would most want robots to do. That's what keeps him awake.
S2.do: Saves about a third more each month straight away and talks to Bea about a smaller wedding. Takes a decent early package if offered in the first year and looks at using his live-line training to check or certify robot crews.
S2.feel: Properly anxious, though not falling apart.
S2.quote: Bea would understand, she's sensible, but I'd feel I'd let her down.
S2.fieldNote: His sense of safety flips here: the danger in his work is what makes it a prime target for robots. He'd shrink his daughter's wedding and feel he'd let her down. He still sees a possible role certifying robot crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to do this properly if people get on with it. Companies should train staff, the government should set safety rules, and workers should be willing to learn. Everyone does their bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's tighter than I'd like but probably all right. I'd be 63, right at my retirement date, so I'd likely just miss it. The worry would be if they started cutting crews a couple of years early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep saving a bit more than now, nothing drastic. Once the robot systems had been tried at a few depots, I'd learn how to supervise them, because that would make me useful for my last couple of years. I'd also keep my live-line certificates up to date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in control.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does having five years change the wedding plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the wedding goes ahead as planned, it's next spring. Five years gives us time to rebuild the savings afterwards. That's the difference, really, time to recover.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be 63 when it arrives. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it sits fine. I'd be leaving at the right time. I'd feel for the younger ones, but it's not a disaster for me.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough if people get on with it: companies train staff, government sets safety rules and workers are willing to learn. Everyone does their bit.
S3.think: It's tighter than he'd like but probably all right, since he'd be 63 and right at his retirement date. His worry is crews being cut a couple of years early.
S3.do: Saves a bit more than now and learns to supervise robot systems once a few depots have tried them. Keeps his live-line certificates up to date.
S3.quote: Five years gives us time to rebuild the savings afterwards. That's the difference, really, time to recover.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years let the wedding go ahead and give him time to rebuild savings. He sees learning to supervise robots as a way to stay useful at the end. His centre outlook shows in giving everyone a share of the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time, so let's plan sensibly and stop panicking. I'd say the same thing to the young crew and to my mates at the club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm retired by then, so it hardly touches me. I'd be 68. Ana and I would be fine on the pension, as long as nothing strange happens to pensions.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on as normal and retire at 63. I'd pick up whatever tools come along in those years once they're proven. Keep saving, enjoy the wedding, nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Tom, who's an accountant?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to look at it carefully, because accounting is the kind of work these programs might do first. He's sharp, he'll work it out. I'd tell him not to wait until year nine to start.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any part of this you'd welcome?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If machines did the most dangerous live jobs, I'd be glad. I've had two close calls in thirty years, and I still think about the second one. If my old crew never had to have one of those, that would be fine by me.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty of time, so plan sensibly and stop panicking. He'd tell the young crew and his friends at the club the same.
S4.think: He'll be 68 and retired, so it hardly touches him, and he and Ana would be fine on the pension. His only doubt is whether something strange happens to pensions.
S4.do: Carries on as normal and retires at 63, picking up proven tools along the way. Keeps saving and enjoys the wedding without any dramatic change.
S4.quote: I've had two close calls in thirty years, and I still think about the second one.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years leaves him untouched and calm. His concern shifts to his son, an accountant whose work may go first. He'd welcome machines taking the most dangerous live jobs, which he linked to a close call he still remembers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. Live-line work is exactly the sort of dangerous job they'd want a robot for, and I'd be three years short. What would help is a fair early retirement deal for older crew, and proper safety rules for robots near live lines, so they don't rush it and get someone hurt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what people's families think. Ana worries every day I go out on a live job. If a robot took that part, she'd sleep better, even if I'd miss it. It's funny, the thing that frightens me for the job is the thing that would comfort her.

headlineQuote: It's funny, the thing that frightens me for the job is the thing that would comfort her.
portrait: Karl Reyes is a 58-year-old live-line crew lead on the coast who works on energised wires and is proudest of eleven years without injury. He uses AI now and then and follows a middle path: adopt tools once they're proven, not first and not last. He's calm if AI plateaus and a little uneasy about steady change, but the two-year AGI picture makes him anxious because dangerous live work is exactly what companies would hand to robots, leaving him three years short of retirement and shrinking his daughter's wedding. With five or ten years he settles, saves a bit more and expects to retire on time.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because live-line work is exactly the kind of dangerous job companies would give to robots and he'd be three years short of retirement.
whatWouldHelp: A fair early retirement deal for older crew, and proper safety rules for robots near live lines so nobody rushes it.
